source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh), ch. 10.4 monster-barring experiments
finding: Resolves the monster-barring threshold conflict. The three numbers come from three different experiments. Single-agent runs (sessions 1-24): a barring minimum of up to 30-40% gave good results; higher values were too restrictive. Multi-agent runs (sessions 69-92): the agency behaved as expected at a minimum between 0 and 10%, and the thesis hypothesises 10% for all students. Mixed-threshold runs (sessions 49-68): best average when the three students' minimums summed to 120-150% (40-50% each); 0% correct at 90% each. The coded default in the algorithm text is 15%.
numbers: Group theory, animal taxonomy, number theory. Barring-minimum grid 0..100 in steps of 10; 12 combinations at 30/60/90% in sessions 53-64. Best single session in number theory: session 71 at 10% (both 0 and 1 barred). Number theory sessions 1-24 scored 97% only because no monster was ever proposed.
quote: we hypothesise that using a monster-barring minimum of 10% for all students in the agency, produces the most interesting behaviour
limits: Scored against the author's own list of expected monsters (0, 1; platypus; semigroups/groupoids). Three toy domains, few sessions per cell, no statistics. No threshold transfers to an LLM.
agent_relevance: Do not carry any threshold number. The useful point is the design: the barring rule is a fraction of existing claims the entity breaks, so it needs a store of accepted claims to measure against.

source: Pease (2007) thesis, ch. 10.3 fine-tuning the method of surrender
finding: The only measured study of when to stop repairing a conjecture. Five cheap signals were tried: number of modifications already made, interestingness against a fixed threshold, interestingness against the theory average, plausibility threshold, domain-of-application threshold. Surrender at zero modifications (give up at the first counterexample) was one of the best. Three modifications was the worst. Comparing a conjecture's interestingness with the theory average scored best. A plausibility threshold of 0.7 was the best plausibility setting. Domain-of-application (scope left) was not useful.
numbers: 42 sessions (14 per domain: group theory, animal taxonomy, number theory), 3 students each, 10 individual phases of 20 theory-formation steps. Hierarchy score (desirable minus undesirable cases): interestingness-vs-average 14; compare-to-average true 12; zero modifications 8; plausibility 0.7 scored 7; modifications=3 gave -12.
quote: The best setting for the number of modifications was 0
limits: Outcome is the students' own interestingness scores, so it is circular. Only the animal domain had conjectures judged worth modifying. The thesis says the result is inconclusive for the threshold value.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the candidate cheap signals are relative value (this claim against the average of the open claims) and plausibility (share of known cases that still satisfy it). Remaining scope was not predictive here. The number of repair rounds is a cap, not a predictor. Needs a test with a real outcome measure.

source: Pease (2007) thesis, ch. 12 Theorem Modifier (TM) on TPTP, and ch. 13.1.1 problem of content
finding: Settles the HR step count for TM: 3000 theory-formation steps, with Otter and MACE at 10 seconds each. Of 98 invented non-theorems TM produced a valid modification for 83%, averaging 3.1 modifications each. Of 9 non-theorems already in TPTP it modified 7 (78%). 300 steps does not appear in the thesis. The 'problem of content' (a conjecture narrowed until its domain is tiny) is named as future work and was not measured.
numbers: 98 invented non-theorems made from TPTP theorems by removing axioms, changing quantifiers, variables, constants, bracketing. 83% valid modification; 3.1 modifications per item; 7 of 9 (78%) on real TPTP non-theorems.
quote: it concerns the situation where a conjecture has been specialised to such an extent that its domain of application is severely reduced
limits: A modification only has to be provable by Otter in the restricted domain. No baseline (for example an untyped restriction or a random restriction). 'Valid' means proved, not interesting or non-trivial; the thesis reports a few trivial equivalences as flagged uninteresting. Ring-theory domain only for the worked case.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the 83% figure is the real Theorem Modifier number. A modern prover with an LLM proposing the restriction is untested. Gap 3: no scope-shrinkage threshold exists in the thesis, only the statement of the problem.

source: Pease (2007) thesis, ch. 9.2.2 and 9.7 hidden lemma-incorporation, surprise tests
finding: Gives the exact definitions of the two surprise tests. Type 1 (unexpected behaviour): an entity x is surprising for conjecture P->Q if there is another conjecture C of form P->Q&R for which x is the only counterexample. HR walks the ancestor (construction) list of Q to find R. Type 2 (non-meaningful terms): entity m is surprising for P(x)->Q(x) if not P(m), i.e. the statement holds only vacuously. Both are shown on one example, Lakatos's cylinder, not on a test set.
numbers: One worked case (cylinder in Euler-characteristic scheme). Ancestor list for Q: [p31_0, p14_0, graph005, poly002]. No success rate reported.
quote: an entity x is surprising with respect to a conjecture P -> Q if there exists another conjecture C such that x is the only counterexample to C
limits: Single worked example, constructed to match Lakatos. Type 2 only handles one-argument predicates. The thesis itself says a cylinder with the existential reading becomes a local as well as a global counterexample, so the case is partly a matter of interpretation.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: an LLM version is simple to write down. (1) List entities that satisfy the claim but behave differently on a probe variable from all other entities (a lone odd-one-out). (2) Check each proof step for a vacuous antecedent. Neither has been tested with an LLM against the plain question 'what did the proof assume?'.

source: Pease, Lawrence, Budzynska, Corneli, Reed (2017) Lakatos-style collaborative mathematics through dialectical, structured and abstract argumentation, Artificial Intelligence 246:181-219
finding: Opened the publisher record and abstract. The paper turns Lakatos's informal logic into a dialogue game over argument structures, builds structured arguments, induces abstract argumentation frameworks and computes semantics to label arguments acceptable. The record states that each formal step is implemented and shows a worked example of real mathematical collaboration. No quantitative evaluation, benchmark or user study is described. The full PDF could not be downloaded (403 / bot check), so the body text was not read.
numbers: No figures given. Semantic Scholar lists 35 citations (Oct 2026).
limits: Abstract page only. Evaluation is by implementation and worked example. Not tested against any baseline and not tested with a language model.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays mostly open. The multi-agent challenge and response idea has a formal semantics but no measured benefit. For our agent it supports a cheap design only: keep a graph of claims, counterexamples and objections, and label what stands. Do not expect measured gains.

source: Repair, Retry, and the Cost of Hindsight: Verifier Feedback in Formal Theorem Proving (arXiv 2610.22698)
finding: On Lean, giving the model its failed proof plus a correct verifier diagnostic helps repair but never beats a fresh memoryless attempt at the same budget. The theorem statement cannot drift because the verifier rebuilds the proof from the dataset statement. Repair prompts are about 80 times longer in input tokens than a fresh draw.
numbers: MiniF2F-test. One step, pass@4: Qwen3.6-27B 45/167 retry vs 40/167 repair; DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B 34/137 retry vs 12/137 repair. Sequential pass@64, 11 problems x 10 trajectories per model: Qwen 44.5% repair vs 62.8% retry (-18.3 pp); DeepSeek 24.5% vs 75.3% (-50.7 pp). Equal 200k total tokens: repair trails by 25.9 pp (Qwen, CI -50.4 to -2.4) and 73.5 pp (DeepSeek). Input per repair attempt about 9.1k vs 115 tokens.
quote: A diagnostic can be useful for repairing a failed proof without making repair better than a new attempt.
limits: Preprint. Only 11 sequential problems per model so intervals are wide. Formal Lean proofs, small models, thinking off for Qwen. Exact repeat of a prior proof body in 73.9% of Qwen no-diagnostic and 65.7% of correct-diagnostic attempts.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 2: the restart control is the strong baseline. Any typed-repair loop of ours must be compared with fresh restarts at equal tokens, counting input tokens. Surrender plus restart is a real competitor to repair.

source: Repair, Retry (arXiv 2610.22698), second half: repair success by attempt and by diagnostic kind
finding: Looks for a signal for when repair pays. Repair helps most when the diagnostic is specific and local. Where Qwen's predecessor proof used Lean 3 syntax, the correct diagnostic added 34.0 pp; elsewhere only 4.3 pp. Where the diagnostic named an unknown identifier it added 26.5 pp; elsewhere 4.0 pp. Even on that subset, repair (29 solved) trailed plain retry (35). The paper tests no stop rule.
numbers: Qwen k=64 cumulative solves: correct diagnostic 49, shuffled diagnostic 29, wrong-match 23, none 25. C_E minus shuffled +18.2 pp [+8.2, +28.2]. DeepSeek: all contrasts about 0 (CI spans zero). Qwen repair-arm conditional fix rate peaks at attempts 3-4 (17.2%) then stays 6-8%.
limits: Conditional rates were computed by the reader from cumulative counts in the paper, not reported by the authors. Exploratory subgroups. 11 problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a candidate cheap signal is the type of the error. Mechanical, local errors (naming, syntax) are repair-worthy; others should restart. This matches Lakatos's local versus global split but was not tested that way.

source: Pythagoras-Prover (2026) Advancing Efficient Formal Proving via Augmented Lean Formalisation (arXiv 2606.12594)
finding: A second source that restart sampling overtakes self-correction as the budget grows. On PutnamBench, a self-correcting prover is ahead at small budgets, then independent restarts pass it. The authors say self-correction becomes brittle when the first attempt has an early logical error that later rounds inherit.
numbers: PutnamBench: Goedel-Prover-V2 with self-correction solves 57 at pass@32 vs Pythagoras-Prover 48; Pythagoras 59 at pass@64 and 93 at pass@2048; Goedel-V2 with self-correction 86 at pass@184. MiniF2F-test 93.0% for the 32B model; 88.1% vs 87.9% at pass@1024 compared with self-correction.
limits: Different models and training in each arm, so the comparison is system against system, not a clean ablation. The appendix claim about inherited early errors was not re-read.
agent_relevance: Supports d06: repair wins early and loses late. The agent should repair for a few rounds and then restart from a fresh draw, which is the engineering form of surrender.

source: Chen et al. ProcessBench (2024) Identifying process errors in mathematical reasoning (arXiv 2412.06559)
finding: Prompted language models can locate the earliest wrong step in a written solution without any executor, and do so better than trained process reward models, but accuracy falls with problem difficulty. Reasoning models do much better than chat models.
numbers: 3,400 test cases from GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH; doctoral-level annotators, at least 3 agreeing, 30% of solutions discarded for no agreement. Metric: F1 of accuracy on erroneous and correct samples. GPT-4o-0806 F1: GSM8K 79.2, MATH 63.6, OlympiadBench 51.4. o1-mini: 93.2, 88.9, 87.2. Open critics use majority vote over 8 samples.
quote: existing PRMs typically underperform the top prompt-driven critic models even on the simpler GSM8K and MATH subsets
limits: Garbled table in the extracted text; the Omni-MATH and average columns were not read cleanly. Math word solutions, not proofs with hidden lemmas. Dec 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: locating the first failing step by reading is feasible but weak for strong chat models on hard problems (about 51 F1 for GPT-4o on olympiad level). Reasoning-mode models are far better. Cost is one long critique per solution.

source: FaithSieve (2026) Fine-grained evaluation of math proofs with faithful formal evidence (arXiv 2608.26310)
finding: Directly answers gap 4 with token matching. Finding the first wrong step by reading only (natural language) is clearly worse than finding it with formal (Lean) evidence, even when the reading-only methods get many more samples. But the formal pipeline costs about 150 times the tokens of a single direct judgement.
numbers: ProofLoc-Olympiad (350 problems, 153 correct and 197 incorrect proofs), GPT-5.4: direct judge 72.29% exact first-error vs FaithSieve 81.43%. ProofLoc-University (200): 75.0 vs 84.5; direct@5 76.0; two critics plus adjudicator 76.0. BIG-Bench Mistake subset (200) with Qwen3.5-9B: FaithSieve 61.0; direct 51.0; majority vote of 241 samples 51.0; context-isolated reviewer panel 52.0 at 100% of FaithSieve's tokens; natural-language decomposition plus challenge and defence 55.5 at 124% of the tokens. Tokens per problem for Qwen: 1,078 direct vs 164,025 FaithSieve (ratio 152). Ablation: without semantic gate GPT-5.4 falls 81.43 to 70.86 exact.
quote: without faithfulness filtering, semantic drift contaminates the final judgment
limits: Preprint, one group, own benchmark. Formal evidence needs autoformalisation, which can itself drift. Strongest NL-only arms at equal tokens gain only 4-5 points over plain judgement.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: independent re-derivation or more reading votes does not close the gap to an executor. A challenge-and-defence structure helped most among NL-only methods (+4.5 over direct). Use an executor wherever one exists; where it does not, expect weak localisation.

source: Woodcock, Leite, Sampaio, Wei (2026) Contract-Aware Rescue of a Drifted Isabelle Development (arXiv 2608.18822)
finding: A real, audited case of repair loops quietly changing the claim. An LLM-assisted proof effort built without sorry or axioms, yet an audit found that 16 of the original 100 declarations had changed, including an end-to-end theorem weakened so that it assumed three of its four requirements in its conclusion. A check of changes against a machine-readable edit contract rejected a trivially weakened theorem that Isabelle accepted.
numbers: 9 theories and 10 open obligations grew to a 16-theory build; 23 stable and 36 broken proof states; 84 of 100 declarations unchanged, 16 changed. With the contract tool all 10 scoped obligations were discharged inside the original 9 theories. A co-author replayed it; independent replication is future work.
quote: A repository can compile after weakening a theorem, adding a convenient assumption, changing a definition or import
limits: One system, one project, one team; a case study, not a rate over a seeded set. The tool was designed by the same authors who ran the test. Gives a count of drift, not a drift rate per repair step.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: monster-barring in disguise is real and accumulates through locally reasonable edits. The remedy that worked was a protected-statement check (diff of the claim and assumptions) rather than asking the model to be careful. The rate on a seeded set is still unmeasured.

source: Faithful Autoformalization via Roundtrip Verification and Repair (arXiv 2604.25031)
finding: Repair loops raise formal equivalence much more than they preserve meaning. A round-trip check plus repair raises the number of equivalent encodings a lot, but meaning drift (unrelated or contradicted by a natural-language-inference check) stays at 15-45% across rows. The paper does not test whether repair itself changes faithfulness, because before and after use different rule pools.
numbers: Texas statutes: 150 traffic rules and 77 wildlife rules; Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.2, up to 3 repair rounds. Round-trip equivalence, traffic/Claude 44.7% to 85.3%; wildlife/Claude 62.3% to 85.7%; traffic/GPT 61.3% to 82.7%. NLI drift pooled: 16.2% for equivalent rules vs 28.7% for non-equivalent (ratio 1.78). Baseline before repair 15.1% (39/258) vs 24.1% (47/195). Human check, 25 rules, one annotator: 13 of 14 equivalent rules faithful (93%), 8 of 11 non-equivalent (73%).
limits: Task is statute formalisation, not proof repair; drift judged by an NLI model; single annotator on 25 rules. Not like for like before and after repair.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a statement-fidelity check (round-trip back to words and compare) is a working design but the drift floor is not zero (about 15%) and no study shows repair success is kept. The planned seeded-set test is still needed.

source: The Self-Correction Illusion: LLMs Correct Others but Not Themselves (arXiv 2606.05976)
finding: Claims the failure to self-correct comes from the chat template: the same wrong claim is fixed far more often when it is labelled as coming from outside than when it sits in the model's own turn. Moving the claim to an external role raised correction by 23 to 93 points.
numbers: 10 model families, 13 model-domain cells, 3 domains (GSM8K-style math, synthetic logic, BBH logical deduction), 30 paired tasks per cell, 10,000-sample paired bootstrap. Baseline correction rate 0% to 97% by cell. Wrong claim adopted from own thought about 83% of the time vs at most 3.3% from external role. Math with Qwen-72B: 70% (memory role) vs 16.7%. Self-distrust prompts 0-23.3%. Adding 'treat this as ground truth' raised attack success to 70%.
quote: The failure to self-correct is not a cognitive deficit; it is a chat-template artifact.
limits: Preprint, small cells (30 tasks). Planted errors, not natural ones. The wrong-claim adoption test also shows the opposite risk: an external label can make wrong claims be accepted.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 4: the challenger should see the claim as someone else's work, in a fresh context. This is cheap and supports a separate refute role. Our refute operator should present the draft as a third-party claim.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) REFUTE (arXiv 2502.19414), re-opened for test-bed design
finding: REFUTE contains only incorrect solutions. Every item has a counterexample, so the false-refutation rate (a counterexample offered against a correct claim) cannot be measured on it. The model writes code that outputs an input; a ground-truth checker runs held-out correct solutions. About 35% of random-search samples end with a wrong counterexample, and 86% of those come from wrong brute-force code.
numbers: 35% of all RandSearch samples end in an incorrect counterexample; of these 14% fail test-case validation and 86% wrong brute-force code. Best model solves under 9% of items.
limits: Algorithmic problems with a checker, not proofs. Closed-form scoring means no true-claim items.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: REFUTE is good for measuring whether a refute operator finds real counterexamples at equal tokens but cannot measure false refutations. We must add correct solutions as negatives.

source: Li et al. (2025) COUNTERMATH (arXiv 2502.10454), re-opened for label balance
finding: COUNTERMATH labels each statement True or False and scores judgement with macro F1, so a false refutation shows up as a False-labelled item judged True or the reverse. The dataset is heavily True-labelled (the paper says most statements are True and Figure 3b shows about 88% True), so accuracy would hide false refutations; they use macro F1. Some open math models produce a counterexample for only 18-27% of statements that need one.
numbers: 1,216 statement-rationale pairs across algebra, topology, real analysis, functional analysis; strongest model judgement F1 80.7; MetaMath and rho produce counterexamples in 26.5% and 18.3% of cases with consistency 0.4% and 1.9%.
limits: The 88% True share is read from a pie chart in garbled layout. No explicit false-refutation rate is reported. University-level concept statements, not algorithm tasks, and judged partly by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: COUNTERMATH gives true and false items with a judgement label, so a prompt-only agent's false-refutation rate can be computed on its True items. Report per-class recall, not accuracy.

source: Pastorek (2026) AutoGraphForge (arXiv 2609.03478), re-opened for the counterexample store dynamics
finding: A persistent store of counterexamples used to steer the next round of conjecture generation has diminishing but real returns: the first round gives most new witnesses, then yield collapses, then a fixed point stops the loop. Most refutations come from the stored datasets, not the expensive search. No comparison with rederiving counterexamples every round is made.
numbers: Single-pass baseline: 3,959 candidates, 1,249 refuted (865 by extremal families, 217 random-model graphs, 161 House of Graphs). Five partitions starting from a store of 2,860 graphs. Round 1 added 494-793 witnesses (about 20-28% growth of the store); round 2 added 39-164; round 3 added 3-21. Four partitions stopped at round 5 (a round adding 0), one at round 9. 8,281 raw survivors; merge removed 1,413 refuted by witnesses from other partitions and 346 duplicates, leaving 6,522. Budget 1.22 CPU-years.
limits: No LLM in the generation loop; graph theory with cheap evaluation. No arm that discards the store. A 21% loss at merge (1,759 of 8,281) shows that a store per shard misses witnesses.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the store pays as a cache of refutation tests, and shared stores matter (shards missed 1,413 refutations). The LLM comparison (store vs rederive) is still untested.

source: Pease thesis (2007), ch. 10.4 and ch. 3, plausibility and interestingness definitions used as surrender signals
finding: Plausibility of a conjecture is (e - c)/e, where e is the number of database entities it discusses and c the number of counterexamples; the barring minimum is likewise a share of existing conjectures broken. These are cheap counting signals on a shared store, which the surrender study (d02) then used. Both rely on keeping all known cases and all accepted claims.
numbers: Plausibility example: all primes are odd over numbers 1-20 gives (8-1)/8 = 0.875. Plausibility threshold options 0.7, 0.8, 0.9; 0.7 best.
limits: Counting needs a case base large enough to be informative; the thesis databases held small numbers of entities.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 3: a usable cheap signal is the fraction of stored cases the current (repaired) claim still covers. A claim that covers only a few cases after repeated narrowing is a candidate for surrender. Needs a test.
